Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Extending to 5-class depth estimation (gen-0 through gen-4) reduces LOGO macro F1 from 0.789 to 0.501, a drop of 0.288 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
The degradation is concentrated in middle depths: gen-2 and gen-3 are effectively inseparable (per-class F1 of 0.268 and 0.259, respectively), with adjacent-depth confusions accounting for the majority of errors.
Alternative classifiers---random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451)---all perform comparably, confirming that the bottleneck is feature separability, not classifier choice.
These results establish three classes as the practical granularity ceiling for the current feature set.
Unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within ${\sim}$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}, non-paraphrastic continuation chains retain some signal at gen-4 (F1\,=\,0.423), but the gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains unresolvable with surface and entropy features alone.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
\label{sec:related-detection}

Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests on token-level distributions \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot approaches exploiting reference-model likelihoods \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers over linguistic features \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
Recent work has pursued diverse detection signals: \citet{intrinsic_dimension} use intrinsic dimensionality estimates, \citet{diveye} propose surprisal diversity features directly comparable to our distributional features, and \citet{generator_barrier} characterize the distributional gap between human and model outputs.
\citet{wu_survey_2025} provide the most comprehensive recent survey; see also \citet{jawahar_survey} for an earlier overview.
Commercial systems such as GPTZero provide trained-classifier detection but are non-reproducible due to proprietary model access, precluding controlled baseline comparison; we restrict evaluation to open methods.
A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
Recent efforts extend detection to multi-class settings: \citet{beyond_binary} propose role recognition and involvement measurement to distinguish collaborative human-LLM generation scenarios, and the SemEval-2024 shared task \cite{semeval2024_task8} evaluates multi-generator attribution across domains and languages.
These approaches discriminate among different \emph{sources} (human vs.\ specific models) rather than recursive generation \emph{depth} within a single generator's chain.
Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71 across individual baselines; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.

\paragraph{Source attribution vs.\ depth estimation.}
A related but distinct task is \emph{source attribution}: identifying \emph{which} model generated a given text.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} train multi-class classifiers over stylometric features to distinguish outputs of different generators, and \citet{munir_looking_glass} learn attribution models that generalize across unseen language models.
These methods answer \emph{who} generated the text; depth estimation answers \emph{how many recursive steps} produced it.
The two tasks are orthogonal: a single generator can produce text at any depth, and texts at the same depth may originate from different generators.
Our LOGO evaluation explicitly decouples generator identity from depth by holding out entire generators, ensuring that the classifier learns depth signal rather than generator fingerprints.

\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
\label{sec:related-collapse}

A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.

Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.
\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss analogous to the telephone game.
\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
Our work differs in two respects: we study \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal beyond the attractor bound; and we focus on \emph{estimating} depth from text features rather than characterizing convergence behavior.

\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
\label{sec:related-diversity}

Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
Our surface features---type-token ratio and hapax ratio---instantiate this observation for inference chains, where we show monotonic diversity decline across generation depths without any model retraining.

These features are classical stylometric measures with a long history in authorship attribution \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship}.
\citet{uchendu_attribution} extend stylometric and neural methods to multi-class attribution of text to specific generators.
We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
Sampling strategies also affect diversity; \citet{nucleus_sampling} show that top-$p$ sampling mitigates some degeneration, but our results demonstrate that diversity still declines monotonically across recursive application of the same sampling procedure.

\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
\label{sec:related-provenance}

Scalable data curation relies on quality signals to filter web-crawled corpora.
\citet{dsir} select pretraining data to match a target distribution, \citet{qurating} learn quality scores from LLM judgments, and \citet{ccnet} filter Common Crawl via perplexity-based heuristics.
Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal: it characterizes \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source, orthogonal to content quality per se.

An alternative approach is proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark}, where identifiable patterns are embedded during generation.
However, \citet{chainwash} demonstrate that watermark strength decays across multi-step generation chains, motivating passive post-hoc methods that do not require generator cooperation.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
As LLM outputs accumulate on the web, training corpora increasingly contain recursively generated text of unknown provenance depth.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}---classifying text as human-written (gen-0), first-generation synthetic (gen-1), or deeper (gen-2+)---beyond binary detection.
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this complementarity achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ depth discrimination---excluding gen-0 to avoid shared-seed overlap---($p < 0.001$ vs.\ all baselines) across 6 base-model generators from 3 model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
In our setting, depth-aware data curation does not outperform random subsampling, positioning depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---per-generator F1 ranging from 0.42 to 0.81 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications, and a separate Limitations section addresses scope boundaries.

1	\section*{Limitations}
2	\label{sec:limitations}
3	
4	All six generators are base (pretrained) models.
5	Web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models, whose generation distributions differ from base model continuations.
6	Preliminary instruct experiments show substantial depth-signal degradation: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 for base OLMo-2-1B) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base).
7	Length-controlled analysis reveals that the effect of instruct tuning on surface features is model-dependent: Qwen models retain weakly positive TTR and hapax partial correlations with depth, while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models.
8	Entropy-based depth signals show reversed partial correlations across all three instruct models (partial $\rho$ ranging from +0.103 to +0.364), though length-matched analysis for the smallest model yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification is near chance (F1 $\approx$ 0.5), leaving the interpretation of these residuals ambiguous.
9	Disentangling architecture-dependent surface effects from the residual entropy sign change in instruct-tuned generation is a critical direction for future work.
10	
11	Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
12	Depth signal persists at this scale, but cross-scale classifier transfer incurs a moderate gap (held-out F1\,=\,0.683 vs.\ 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators).
13	Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.
14	
15	We evaluate three prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}) but all share the same Pythia-2.8B generator.
16	Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms the depth signal generalizes, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.
17

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
5	Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
6	One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
7	Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
8	If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
9	Sampling ablation supports this account: depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation (F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades at extreme temperatures ($t = 1.0$, $-6$\,pp), consistent with shape features being determined by the sampling mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
10	We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.
11	
12	\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
13	Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
14	Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
15	This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
16	Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.
17	
18	\paragraph{Practical implications.}
19	The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
20	Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
21	Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
22	Cross-model chain evaluation (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirms that depth signal persists even when chains involve heterogeneous generators, supporting applicability to realistic web-contamination scenarios.
23	Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
24	\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
25	Extending to 5-class depth estimation (gen-0 through gen-4) reduces LOGO macro F1 from 0.789 to 0.501, a drop of 0.288 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
26	The degradation is concentrated in middle depths: gen-2 and gen-3 are effectively inseparable (per-class F1 of 0.268 and 0.259, respectively), with adjacent-depth confusions accounting for the majority of errors.
27	Alternative classifiers---random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451)---all perform comparably, confirming that the bottleneck is feature separability, not classifier choice.
28	These results establish three classes as the practical granularity ceiling for the current feature set.
29	Unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within ${\sim}$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}, non-paraphrastic continuation chains retain some signal at gen-4 (F1\,=\,0.423), but the gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains unresolvable with surface and entropy features alone.
30	End-to-end fine-tuning (QLoRA on Qwen3-0.6B) raises the 3-class ceiling to F1\,=\,0.905 (+11.6\,pp over handcrafted features; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that raw embeddings contain exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.
31	
32	\paragraph{Paraphrastic contamination control.}
33	Initial paraphrastic chain experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), raising concern that depth signal might be confounded by data contamination from continuation-style seeds leaking into paraphrastic chains.
34	After removing contaminated samples, paraphrastic entropy correlations align with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
35	On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with the faster convergence predicted by \citet{broken_telephone}.
36	Cross-transfer remains effective: a classifier trained on paraphrastic chains achieves binary F1\,=\,0.770 on continuation data, and the reverse transfer yields 0.743, indicating that depth features capture a shared distributional signal across chain types despite differing convergence rates.
37	
38	\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
39	Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
40	LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
41	This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.
42	
43	\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
44	Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
45	This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
46	The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.
47	
48	\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
49	Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
50	Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
51	We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
52	This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
53	The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.
54	
55	\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
56	Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
57	However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
58	Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary synthetic text detection, providing a framework for characterizing the provenance of web-crawled text at finer granularity.
Across six generators from three model families (0.6B--8.2B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency and diversity features drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features remain near-stationary.
A 7-feature ensemble combining both feature types achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination across six base-model generators, with per-generator std of 0.051.
Cross-model chains---where each generation step uses a different generator---yield comparable performance (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), confirming that depth signal persists under the generator heterogeneity typical of real-world contamination.
We also reported that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling, establishing that, in our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting functions as a diagnostic tool for provenance characterization rather than a curative tool for data selection.

Future work should extend evaluation to instruction-tuned and RLHF models, frontier-scale generators (70B+), and multilingual settings.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

Adjacent depths (gen-2$\leftrightarrow$gen-3, gen-3$\leftrightarrow$gen-4) account for the majority of errors, consistent with the intuition that deeper recursive generations converge in surface-level statistical fingerprints.
Gen-0 (human text) remains highly distinguishable (F1 = 0.921), and gen-1 retains moderate separability (F1 = 0.634).
Notably, shape features that are near-stationary in the 3-class setting become substantially more important under 5-class evaluation: permutation importance of entropy\_std increases by 93\% and tail\_decay by 400\% relative to 3-class, yet these gains are insufficient to resolve adjacent depths.
These results support the 3-class grouping adopted in the main paper: collapsing gen-2+ preserves the most informative boundary (human vs.\ first-generation vs.\ deeper recursion) while avoiding the noise introduced by near-identical adjacent depths.

\paragraph{Classifier comparison.}
To verify that 5-class degradation reflects feature-level limitations rather than classifier choice, we evaluate four alternatives under the same protocol: HistGradientBoosting (macro F1\,=\,0.501, 95\% bootstrap CI [0.496, 0.506]), random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451).
All classifiers perform comparably to the default XGBoost ensemble (0.501), ruling out classifier capacity as the bottleneck.
The gen-2/gen-3 boundary is the primary failure mode across all methods: these two classes are effectively inseparable with the current feature set, establishing 3-class granularity as the practical ceiling for surface and entropy features.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All six generators are base (pretrained) models.
Web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models, whose generation distributions differ from base model continuations.
Preliminary instruct experiments show substantial depth-signal degradation: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 for base OLMo-2-1B) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 base).
Length-controlled analysis reveals that the effect of instruct tuning on surface features is model-dependent: Qwen models retain weakly positive TTR and hapax partial correlations with depth, while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models.
Entropy-based depth signals show reversed partial correlations across all three instruct models (partial $\rho$ ranging from +0.103 to +0.364), though length-matched analysis for the smallest model yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification is near chance (F1 $\approx$ 0.5), leaving the interpretation of these residuals ambiguous.
Disentangling architecture-dependent surface effects from the residual entropy sign change in instruct-tuned generation is a critical direction for future work.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale, but cross-scale classifier transfer incurs a moderate gap (held-out F1\,=\,0.683 vs.\ 0.76--0.86 for $\leq$2.8B generators).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

We evaluate three prompt types (continuation, elaboration, rewriting; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}) but all share the same Pythia-2.8B generator.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms the depth signal generalizes, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm that depth signal persists under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the six generators tested represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of web-scale contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation under casual editing, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world human post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) suggest the phenomenon is not reference-specific.
All seed texts are English Wikipedia excerpts; generalization to other languages and domains remains untested.

The negative downstream result (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}) is evaluated on causal language modeling only.
Other downstream tasks (classification, summarization, instruction following) may respond differently to depth composition.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
Sampling ablation supports this account: depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation (F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades at extreme temperatures ($t = 1.0$, $-6$\,pp), consistent with shape features being determined by the sampling mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Cross-model chain evaluation (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirms that depth signal persists even when chains involve heterogeneous generators, supporting applicability to realistic web-contamination scenarios.
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Extending to 5-class depth estimation (gen-0 through gen-4) reduces LOGO macro F1 from 0.789 to 0.501, a drop of 0.288 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
The degradation is concentrated in middle depths: gen-2 and gen-3 are effectively inseparable (per-class F1 of 0.268 and 0.259, respectively), with adjacent-depth confusions accounting for the majority of errors.
Alternative classifiers---random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451)---all perform comparably, confirming that the bottleneck is feature separability, not classifier choice.
These results establish three classes as the practical granularity ceiling for the current feature set.
Unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within ${\sim}$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}, non-paraphrastic continuation chains retain some signal at gen-4 (F1\,=\,0.423), but the gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains unresolvable with surface and entropy features alone.
End-to-end fine-tuning (QLoRA on Qwen3-0.6B) raises the 3-class ceiling to F1\,=\,0.905 (+11.6\,pp over handcrafted features; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that raw embeddings contain exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.

\paragraph{Paraphrastic contamination control.}
Initial paraphrastic chain experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), raising concern that depth signal might be confounded by data contamination from continuation-style seeds leaking into paraphrastic chains.
After removing contaminated samples, paraphrastic entropy correlations align with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with the faster convergence predicted by \citet{broken_telephone}.
Cross-transfer remains effective: a classifier trained on paraphrastic chains achieves binary F1\,=\,0.770 on continuation data, and the reverse transfer yields 0.743, indicating that depth features capture a shared distributional signal across chain types despite differing convergence rates.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Reference-model independence.}
The depth signal is not an artifact of reference-model choice.
Overall LOGO F1 varies by only 0.013 across three cross-family reference models (0.803--0.816; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}), and entropy drift direction is consistently negative for all three, confirming that the differential depth response is a property of recursive generation itself.
At the per-generator level, Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M); cross-family references yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), ruling out family bias as an explanation for its high detectability.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
Length-controlled analysis reveals a consistent pattern.
Entropy-based features reverse sign across all three instruct models (partial $\rho$ = +0.103, +0.161, +0.364 for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and OLMo-Instruct respectively), though the interpretation is complicated by severe length confounds.
Qwen3-0.6B exhibits the weakest residual (+0.103), and a stricter length-matched robustness check yields near-zero correlations (all length-matched $|\rho| < 0.02$), consistent with the depth--feature association being largely mediated by the extreme length disparity across depths (252 vs.\ 23 tokens for gen-0 vs.\ gen-2+).
Qwen3-1.7B partial correlations are also substantially reduced after length matching (surface features by 53--60\%, entropy by 91\%), and gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ binary classification is near chance for both models (F1 $\approx$ 0.5), indicating that depth signal is not operationally detectable in instruct chains.
OLMo-Instruct's substantially larger residual ($+0.364$) likely reflects differences in alignment recipe rather than parameter count alone.
Surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) show model-dependent behavior: Qwen3-1.7B retains weakly positive partial correlations with depth (TTR partial $\rho$ = +0.130; hapax partial $\rho$ = +0.166), while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models (TTR partial $\rho = -0.241$; hapax partial $\rho = -0.198$).
This divergence cautions against treating surface feature reversal as a universal consequence of instruction tuning; the effect is architecture- or training-recipe-dependent.

OLMo-Instruct presents a paradox: it exhibits the strongest entropy--depth partial correlation (+0.364) yet the worst classification performance (LOGO F1\,=\,0.338).
A likely explanation is that its surface features retain base-model polarity (negative partial $\rho$) while entropy reverses to positive, creating contradictory signals for a classifier trained on base-model patterns---where entropy and surface features are jointly negative at greater depths.
OLMo-Instruct breaks this joint structure, and the resulting signal conflict may account for the classification collapse.
Disentangling these mechanisms across a broader set of instruct models is a priority for future work; the current findings justify restricting our scope to base models where such confounds are minimal.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Why are shape features stationary?}
Distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary across generation depths, while central-tendency features drift monotonically (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
One \emph{speculative} explanation is that shape is primarily determined by the sampling mechanism (temperature, top-$p$ truncation) and the model's architecture-level output distribution, both of which are fixed across generation steps.
Recursive generation shifts \emph{what} the model talks about---steering toward higher-probability vocabulary regions---but does not alter \emph{how} the model distributes probability mass around its predictions.
If this account is correct, shape features should remain stationary even at much greater depths and across different prompt types, while level features should continue to drift until reaching a fixed point.
Sampling ablation supports this account: depth signal is robust to moderate sampling variation (F1 range ${\leq}0.3$\,pp for $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$) but degrades at extreme temperatures ($t = 1.0$, $-6$\,pp), consistent with shape features being determined by the sampling mechanism (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
We flag this as a hypothesis for future investigation, not a conclusion supported by our current experiments.

\paragraph{Relation to OOD detection.}
Reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores---the same signal backbone underlying DetectGPT \cite{detectgpt}, GLTR \cite{gltr}, and Binoculars \cite{binoculars}.
Our contribution is not these features per se, but the \emph{ordinal} depth formulation and the empirical finding that they exhibit differential depth response under recursive generation.
This connection also offers a lens on shape stationarity: in the OOD detection literature, distributional location statistics (mean log-likelihood) shift under domain drift, while shape statistics (variance, tail behavior) are more robust \cite{ood_baseline}.
Recursive generation chains produce an analogous effect---progressive drift away from human text that manifests primarily as a location shift in the NLL distribution.

\paragraph{Practical implications.}
The differential depth response enables provenance characterization of text corpora.
Rather than binary keep-or-discard filtering, practitioners can use depth estimates to understand the composition of their data.
Whether this understanding translates to improved curation outcomes remains an open question (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
Cross-model chain evaluation (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirms that depth signal persists even when chains involve heterogeneous generators, supporting applicability to realistic web-contamination scenarios.
Three-class granularity separates human text from moderate-drift first-generation content and from deeper text with compounding distributional shift---the distinction most relevant to provenance analysis.
\paragraph{Granularity ceiling.}
Extending to 5-class depth estimation (gen-0 through gen-4) reduces LOGO macro F1 from 0.789 to 0.501, a drop of 0.288 (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}).
The degradation is concentrated in middle depths: gen-2 and gen-3 are effectively inseparable (per-class F1 of 0.268 and 0.259, respectively), with adjacent-depth confusions accounting for the majority of errors.
Alternative classifiers---random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451)---all perform comparably, confirming that the bottleneck is feature separability, not classifier choice.
These results establish three classes as the practical granularity ceiling for the current feature set.
Unlike paraphrastic chains, which converge within ${\sim}$3 steps \cite{broken_telephone}, non-paraphrastic continuation chains retain some signal at gen-4 (F1\,=\,0.423), but the gen-2/gen-3 boundary remains unresolvable with surface and entropy features alone.
End-to-end fine-tuning (QLoRA on Qwen3-0.6B) raises the 3-class ceiling to F1\,=\,0.905 (+11.6\,pp over handcrafted features; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that raw embeddings contain exploitable depth signal beyond summary statistics.

\paragraph{Paraphrastic contamination control.}
Initial paraphrastic chain experiments exhibited reversed entropy--depth correlations ($\rho = +0.394$), raising concern that depth signal might be confounded by data contamination from continuation-style seeds leaking into paraphrastic chains.
After removing contaminated samples, paraphrastic entropy correlations align with continuation chains ($\rho = -0.533$), confirming the reversal was an artifact.
On clean data, paraphrastic chains achieve binary F1\,=\,0.671 (vs.\ 0.749 for continuation), consistent with the faster convergence predicted by \citet{broken_telephone}.
Cross-transfer remains effective: a classifier trained on paraphrastic chains achieves binary F1\,=\,0.770 on continuation data, and the reverse transfer yields 0.743, indicating that depth features capture a shared distributional signal across chain types despite differing convergence rates.

\paragraph{Robustness to post-generation editing.}
Depth features degrade gracefully under simulated human editing: random token replacement at 20\% reduces 3-class F1 by only 6.0\,pp while binary F1 (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) remains nearly unchanged ($\Delta \leq 0.8$\,pp).
LLM rephrasing presents a different challenge---3-class degradation is modest ($-3.4$\,pp), but binary F1 drops 6.3\,pp, indicating that systematic distributional manipulation erodes depth signal more effectively than surface noise (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
This asymmetry has practical implications: depth fingerprinting is robust to casual editing but more vulnerable in settings where LLM-assisted rewriting is prevalent.

\paragraph{Information value of the negative finding.}
Depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count (\S\ref{sec:results-downstream}).
This negative result carries positive information value: it rules out depth-based filtering as a data selection strategy, sparing practitioners from building depth-conditional pipelines that would not yield quality gains.
The dominant factor is data quantity, not depth composition---consistent with findings emphasizing data volume over curation sophistication \cite{self_consuming_mad}.

\paragraph{Connection to model collapse.}
Our results relate to, but are distinct from, model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse,self_consuming_mad}.
Model collapse describes distributional degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs across generations.
We observe analogous drift---monotonic decrease in vocabulary diversity, compression of perplexity---in \emph{inference chains} without any parameter updates.
This suggests that the mechanisms documented in model collapse theory (regression toward high-probability modes, loss of distributional tails) operate at inference time as well, driven by the sampling process rather than gradient updates.
The shared phenomenology motivates using depth fingerprinting features as early indicators of data that, if fed back into training, may accelerate model collapse.

\paragraph{Topic drift as mediator, not confounder.}
Recursive generation narrows topic diversity: cosine similarity between adjacent depths increases monotonically from 0.62 (depth 0$\to$1) to 0.86 (depth 3$\to$4), consistent with regression toward high-probability modes.
However, topic narrowing accounts for less than 9\% of feature variance (maximum: entropy\_mean, $\rho = -0.286$, $R^2 = 0.082$).
Shape features are near-independent of semantic drift (tail\_decay $|\rho| = 0.068$, $R^2 = 0.005$).
Topic drift is best understood as a \emph{mediator}---one mechanism through which depth manifests---rather than a confound that invalidates depth features.
The depth signal primarily reflects sampling-induced distributional compression, not topic narrowing per se.

\paragraph{Depth features vs.\ multi-detector ensembles.}
In 3-class evaluation, multi-detector ensembles achieve marginally higher F1 (0.805 with surface features added vs.\ 0.789).
However, this advantage is driven entirely by gen-0 classification, where detection scores excel at human-vs-machine discrimination.
In the leak-free binary evaluation (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), the 7-feature ensemble matches the best multi-detector configuration (0.723 vs.\ 0.724), demonstrating that depth features capture the gen-1/gen-2+ distinction as effectively as four detection pipelines combined.
Depth features additionally offer interpretability---they reveal the differential depth response pattern---and computational efficiency, requiring only a single lightweight reference model.

\paragraph{Reference-model independence.}
The depth signal is not an artifact of reference-model choice.
Overall LOGO F1 varies by only 0.013 across three cross-family reference models (0.803--0.816; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}), and entropy drift direction is consistently negative for all three, confirming that the differential depth response is a property of recursive generation itself.
At the per-generator level, Pythia-1B achieves the highest held-out F1 (0.856) despite using a same-family reference model (Pythia-410M); cross-family references yield nearly identical Pythia-1B F1 (0.845--0.848), ruling out family bias as an explanation for its high detectability.

\paragraph{Instruct tuning degrades depth signal through multiple mechanisms.}
Preliminary experiments with instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker depth fingerprints: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 for base OLMo-2-1B), and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template yields F1\,=\,0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 for the base model).
Length-controlled analysis reveals a consistent pattern.
Entropy-based features reverse sign across all three instruct models (partial $\rho$ = +0.103, +0.161, +0.364 for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-1.7B, and OLMo-Instruct respectively), suggesting a genuine shift in the generation process that survives length control.
Qwen3-0.6B exhibits the weakest reversal (+0.103); a stricter length-matched robustness check yields near-zero correlations (all length-matched $|\rho| < 0.02$), likely because its extreme length disparity across depths (252 vs.\ 23 tokens) causes length-matching to discard the majority of samples rather than indicating a true absence of signal.
OLMo-Instruct's substantially larger residual ($+0.364$) likely reflects differences in alignment recipe rather than parameter count alone.
Surface features (TTR, hapax ratio) show model-dependent behavior: Qwen3-1.7B retains weakly positive partial correlations with depth (TTR partial $\rho$ = +0.130; hapax partial $\rho$ = +0.166), while OLMo-Instruct exhibits negative correlations similar to base models (TTR partial $\rho = -0.241$; hapax partial $\rho = -0.198$).
This divergence cautions against treating surface feature reversal as a universal consequence of instruction tuning; the effect is architecture- or training-recipe-dependent.

OLMo-Instruct presents a paradox: it exhibits the strongest entropy--depth partial correlation (+0.364) yet the worst classification performance (LOGO F1\,=\,0.338).
A likely explanation is that its surface features retain base-model polarity (negative partial $\rho$) while entropy reverses to positive, creating contradictory signals for a classifier trained on base-model patterns---where entropy and surface features are jointly negative at greater depths.
OLMo-Instruct breaks this joint structure, and the resulting signal conflict may account for the classification collapse.
Disentangling these mechanisms across a broader set of instruct models is a priority for future work; the current findings justify restricting our scope to base models where such confounds are minimal.

We evaluate finer-grained 5-class depth classification (gen-0 through gen-4) using the same 7-feature ensemble and LOGO protocol described in \S\ref{sec:method}.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Held-out Generator} & \textbf{Macro F1} & \textbf{Weighted F1} & \textbf{Accuracy} \\
\midrule
OLMo-2-1B       & 0.484 & 0.506 & 0.524 \\
Pythia-1B        & 0.543 & 0.568 & 0.575 \\
Pythia-2.8B      & 0.523 & 0.540 & 0.560 \\
Qwen3-0.6B      & 0.513 & 0.521 & 0.546 \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & 0.510 & 0.536 & 0.548 \\
Qwen3-8B        & 0.434 & 0.455 & 0.493 \\
\midrule
\textbf{Average} & \textbf{0.501 $\pm$ 0.038} & \textbf{0.521} & \textbf{0.541} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{5-class LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out one generator for testing, training on the remaining five.}
\label{tab:5class-logo}
\end{table}

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{lccccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Metric} & \textbf{Gen-0} & \textbf{Gen-1} & \textbf{Gen-2} & \textbf{Gen-3} & \textbf{Gen-4} \\
\midrule
Avg F1      & 0.921 & 0.634 & 0.268 & 0.259 & 0.423 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Per-class F1 averaged across all six LOGO folds.}
\label{tab:5class-perclass}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Analysis.}
Moving from 3-class (gen-0 / gen-1 / gen-2+) to 5-class classification reduces LOGO macro F1 from 0.789 to 0.501, a drop of 0.288.
The degradation is concentrated in the middle depths: gen-2 and gen-3 achieve only 0.268 and 0.259 F1, respectively.
The aggregated confusion matrix reveals that 36.5\% of true gen-2 samples are misclassified as gen-1, while 37.8\% of true gen-3 samples are predicted as gen-4.
Adjacent depths (gen-2$\leftrightarrow$gen-3, gen-3$\leftrightarrow$gen-4) account for the majority of errors, consistent with the intuition that deeper recursive generations converge in surface-level statistical fingerprints.
Gen-0 (human text) remains highly distinguishable (F1 = 0.921), and gen-1 retains moderate separability (F1 = 0.634).
Notably, shape features that are near-stationary in the 3-class setting become substantially more important under 5-class evaluation: permutation importance of entropy\_std increases by 93\% and tail\_decay by 400\% relative to 3-class, yet these gains are insufficient to resolve adjacent depths.
These results support the 3-class grouping adopted in the main paper: collapsing gen-2+ preserves the most informative boundary (human vs.\ first-generation vs.\ deeper recursion) while avoiding the noise introduced by near-identical adjacent depths.

\paragraph{Classifier comparison.}
To verify that 5-class degradation reflects feature-level limitations rather than classifier choice, we evaluate four alternatives under the same protocol: HistGradientBoosting (macro F1\,=\,0.501, 95\% bootstrap CI [0.496, 0.506]), random forest (0.476), logistic regression (0.447), and Frank-Hall ordinal reduction (0.451).
All classifiers perform comparably to the default XGBoost ensemble (0.501), ruling out classifier capacity as the bottleneck.
The gen-2/gen-3 boundary is the primary failure mode across all methods: these two classes are effectively inseparable with the current feature set, establishing 3-class granularity as the practical ceiling for surface and entropy features.

9	\citet{wu_survey_2025} provide the most comprehensive recent survey; see also \citet{jawahar_survey} for an earlier overview.
10	Commercial systems such as GPTZero provide trained-classifier detection but are non-reproducible due to proprietary model access, precluding controlled baseline comparison; we restrict evaluation to open methods.
11	A persistent limitation is that all these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
12	Recent efforts extend detection to multi-class settings: \citet{beyond_binary} propose role recognition and involvement measurement to distinguish collaborative human-LLM generation scenarios, and the SemEval-2024 shared task \cite{semeval2024_task8} evaluates multi-generator attribution across domains and languages.
13	These approaches discriminate among different \emph{sources} (human vs.\ specific models) rather than recursive generation \emph{depth} within a single generator's chain.
14	Even when detection scores correlate with generation depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance when repurposed as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71 across individual baselines; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each score captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently.
15	\citet{paraphrase_evades} and \citet{detection_possibilities} further demonstrate that detection robustness degrades under distributional shift.
16	Our reference-model entropy features are functionally NLL-based out-of-distribution scores \cite{ood_baseline}; the contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the empirical finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
17	
18	\paragraph{Source attribution vs.\ depth estimation.}
19	A related but distinct task is \emph{source attribution}: identifying \emph{which} model generated a given text.
20	\citet{uchendu_attribution} train multi-class classifiers over stylometric features to distinguish outputs of different generators, and \citet{munir_looking_glass} learn attribution models that generalize across unseen language models.
21	These methods answer \emph{who} generated the text; depth estimation answers \emph{how many recursive steps} produced it.
22	The two tasks are orthogonal: a single generator can produce text at any depth, and texts at the same depth may originate from different generators.
23	Our LOGO evaluation explicitly decouples generator identity from depth by holding out entire generators, ensuring that the classifier learns depth signal rather than generator fingerprints.
24	
25	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
26	\label{sec:related-collapse}
27	
28	A growing body of work studies quality degradation when models are trained on their own outputs.
29	\citet{self_consuming_mad} demonstrate that self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage, and \citet{curse_of_recursion} show that model collapse is inevitable in successive fine-tuning rounds without fresh human data, though \citet{model_collapse_avoidable} identify conditions under which careful data mixing can mitigate this effect.
30	\citet{strong_model_collapse} extend these results to larger-scale settings.
31	These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation, where model weights are updated on recursive data.
32	Our setting is different: we study \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
33	
34	Two concurrent lines of work are most directly relevant.

36	\citet{markovian_chains} provide a theoretical framework for convergence in iterative text transformations, demonstrating that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics that bound distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.

38

47	We push beyond generator identity to the \emph{depth} dimension: text from the same generator at different depths exhibits systematically different feature profiles, and these profiles generalize across generators.
48	Sampling strategies also affect diversity; \citet{nucleus_sampling} show that top-$p$ sampling mitigates some degeneration, but our results demonstrate that diversity still declines monotonically across recursive application of the same sampling procedure.
49

51	\label{sec:related-provenance}
52	
53	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals to filter web-crawled corpora.
54	\citet{dsir} select pretraining data to match a target distribution, \citet{qurating} learn quality scores from LLM judgments, and \citet{ccnet} filter Common Crawl via perplexity-based heuristics.
55	Generation depth is a complementary provenance signal: it characterizes \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source, orthogonal to content quality per se.
56	
57	An alternative approach is proactive provenance through watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark}, where identifiable patterns are embedded during generation.
58	However, \citet{chainwash} demonstrate that watermark strength decays across multi-step generation chains, motivating passive post-hoc methods that do not require generator cooperation.
59	Our depth fingerprinting is such a method: it operates on text alone without assuming access to the generating model or an embedded watermark.
60	At the feature level, our reference-model NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability distribution's lower tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for a different purpose---ordinal depth estimation rather than training-set membership.

1	\section{Introduction}
2	\label{sec:introduction}
3	
4	Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
5	Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
6	The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.
7	
8	Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
9	This conflates qualitatively different material.
10	A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
11	A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
12	Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.
13	
14	We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
15	We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
16	No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
17	When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---per-generator F1 ranging from 0.42 to 0.81 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
18	Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
19	These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
20	We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).
21	
22	We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
23	We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
24	This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
25	The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
26	
27	We also report a negative finding.
28	Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
29	In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.
30	
31	Our contributions are:
32	\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
33	    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
34	    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
35	    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.
36	\end{enumerate}
37	
38	The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
39	\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora are the dominant source of pretraining data for large language models (LLMs), yet an increasing fraction of this data is itself LLM-generated.
Estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}, and this proportion continues to grow as generated text enters the web and becomes seed material for subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text---a problem that current detection methods are ill-equipped to address.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt} provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, forcing an all-or-nothing filtering decision: discard everything flagged as synthetic, losing potentially useful first-generation content, or retain everything, admitting text with compounding distributional drift.
This conflates qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation---an LLM expanding a human-written passage---retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties.
A third- or fourth-generation text, conditioned recursively on prior LLM outputs, exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity, compressed perplexity, and narrower token probability distributions.
Treating these as a single ``synthetic'' category discards provenance information that could inform risk-stratified curation decisions.

We argue that a finer-grained characterization is needed: \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, the task of classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label.
We refer to the overall framework---features, classifier, and evaluation protocol---as \emph{depth fingerprinting}, distinguishing the method from the task it addresses.
No existing method addresses this task directly in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores exhibit high cross-generator variance---per-generator F1 ranging from 0.42 to 0.81 (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines})---making any single detector unreliable across unknown generators.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence behavior under semantic-preservation constraints, which bound distinguishable depth classes to approximately three.
These results do not extend to \emph{non-paraphrastic} generation chains (e.g., continuation), where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.
We focus on non-paraphrastic continuation chains from base (pretrained) models; instruction-tuned and RLHF models, which dominate web text, remain untested (Limitations).

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic LLM generation chains across six generators from three model families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen; 0.6B--8.2B parameters).
We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features---including reference-model mean entropy (functionally an NLL-based out-of-distribution score \cite{ood_baseline}), type-token ratio, and hapax ratio---drift monotonically with generation depth, while distributional shape features (entropy standard deviation, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
This pattern is consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution: text becomes progressively more predictable on average while the functional form of the distribution is preserved.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves binary macro-F1 of 0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).

We also report a negative finding.
Depth-aware data curation---selecting training data based on estimated generation depth---does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 random vs.\ 2.387 depth-stratified).
In our experimental setting, depth fingerprinting is an effective \emph{diagnostic} tool for characterizing text provenance, not a \emph{curative} tool for data selection.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for finer-grained provenance characterization of web-crawled text.
    \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We characterize differential depth response across six base-model generators spanning three model families (0.6B--8.2B): a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves binary F1\,=\,0.723 (95\% CI: [0.717, 0.729]) for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$), with per-generator consistency (std\,=\,0.051).
    \item \textbf{Complementary analysis.} As a complementary analysis, we show that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling, establishing depth fingerprinting as a diagnostic rather than curative tool.
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, baseline comparisons, and the downstream utility experiment.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications, and a separate Limitations section addresses scope boundaries.
